name: Sakha Republic
summary_text: Visitors in the Sakha Republic stand under the national framework of Russia, where consensual same-sex activity is not criminalised but same-sex marriage and gender transition are banned. The Supreme Court designated the international LGBT+ movement an extremist organisation in November 2023, trans-specific healthcare was effectively banned in 2023, and 'gay propaganda' offences carry fines of up to 400,000 rubles (about £3,600) or 15 days' detention for individuals. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) is the framework against which this division is scored, and it contains no division-specific information beyond that national picture.  The only Sakha-specific incident on record is documented by Human Rights Watch (30 June 2025): in November 2024 a court in Yakutsk imposed an additional sentence on a prisoner for allegedly showing the rainbow flag to other prisoners. Display of the flag inside a detention facility was treated as an aggravating act warranting extra punishment, which indicates that the extremist-designation regime is applied by courts in the republic and not only in the western regions of Russia.  Enforcement volume nationally is documented in the same reporting. Russian courts have issued 101 extremism-related convictions since the November 2023 designation, with defendants facing up to 12 years in prison, and Human Rights Watch documented 81 people across 98 cases found guilty since January 2024 of article 20.3 administrative offences for displaying banned symbols, most of them based on social media posts. Between 2022 and 2024 at least 139 individuals were affected by anti-LGBT+ law enforcement in Russia.

name: Tatarstan
summary_text: Tatarstan stands under the national framework of Russia, where legal gender recognition and gender-affirming care were banned outright in 2023, the Supreme Court has designated the "international LGBT movement" an extremist organisation, and the expanded propaganda law criminalises public expression that includes anything "justifying" gender transition. Foreigners who breach these provisions face arrest, detention of up to 15 days, and deportation.  Same-sex marriage and legal gender transition are prohibited, trans-specific healthcare has been effectively banned since 2023, and no discrimination protection exists. The UK Home Office country policy and information note on sexual orientation and gender identity and expression (June 2025) records at least 139 people impacted by anti-LGBT+ laws across Russia between 2022 and 2024.  Human Rights Watch reported 101 extremism-related convictions by 30 June 2025 for alleged participation in the designated "international LGBT movement" or display of its symbols, comprising 98 administrative and 3 criminal cases. Between January 2024 and June 2025 at least 20 people faced criminal charges under the designation, two sentenced to prison and seventeen pending or unknown.  On 15 May 2025, three staff of two publishing houses were charged with running an extremist organisation under article 282.2 and face up to 12 years in prison. Repeated display of banned symbols is punishable by up to four years in prison.  The UK Home Office note places the elevated state-persecution exception, which covers trans people, public LGBT+ advocates and North Caucasus residents likely to face treatment amounting to persecution, outside ordinary regions such as Tatarstan.
